title: Defence Department tops up cadet program after outrage over cancelled activities
summary: The Defence Department will top up the budget of the cadet and junior ranger programs to allow weekend training and other activities to continue into the new year, Defence Minister David McGuinty…

image.caption: Cadets march in the parade to the cenotaph as part of the Remembrance Day ceremony in Fredericton, on Wednesday, Nov. 11, 2026. (Stephen MacGillivray/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Politics·Breaking

The Defence Department will top up the budget of the cadet and junior ranger programs to allow weekend training and other activities to continue into the new year, Defence Minister David McGuinty said on Monday.
Extra funding will allow weekend training, other activities to continue
The Canadian military put a halt to most cadet training in various parts of the country because of ongoing budget restraint within the department.

The halt involved weekend training and participation in competitions and was supposed to last until the end of the fiscal year in March. Weekly parade nights, however, were slated to continue while the department reviewed program funding.

The decision drew outrage from ordinary Canadians and the Opposition Conservatives. A number of Liberal MPs have privately said they've received a flood of constituent complaints and questions about the Defence Department's spending priorities at a time when billions of extra dollars are being spent on the military.

blocks.text: McGuinty said the cadet program is vital for young people and the government will provide extra funding.
"We've heard your concerns about changes to planned activities," McGuinty said on his way into the House of Commons.
"We can confirm that additional funding will be provided to ensure planned cadet and junior Canadian ranger activities can continue for the remainder of this fiscal year."
It's unclear what the size of the budget bailout will be.
Restoring cadet activities, McGuinty says Canada's defence funding is not 'limitless'

It is an important reversal because just last week, the second-in-command of Canada's military stood behind the decision to pause the training and other activities until March 31 and the new budget year.

Vice-Admiral Angus Topshee told a House of Commons committee that membership in the cadets program has jumped by roughly 20,000 in the last few years and funding for the program has also increased to $265 million annually.
"Unfortunately, a lot of the cadet funding is front-loaded. It happens during the summer months," Topshee said on Thursday.
"And so they spent a large part of that expanded budget on summer training. And we didn't factor in the sizable increase in the number of cadets participating in the program."
Military's 2nd-in-command says increase in cadets led to temporary cuts

He said, despite the growth in the budget, the cadet program had "run up against a hard cap on the amount of money that they've been given" and that it was important for the department to live within its means.
On Monday, McGuinty defended the cadet program's handling of its budget, saying new entrants can walk through the door and sign up at any time and that makes managing the finances a challenge.
"When we look back and we see what the growth has been, it's been considerable," McGuinty said.
He added that a review of precisely how big the cadet program budget needs to be is ongoing.

blocks.text: The initial decision to rein in the cadet program budget was just one part of a series of internal belt-tightening measures at DND.

While the Liberal government has drastically ramped up defence spending and has largely exempted the department from its expenditure review program, it has also told DND to focus its billions of dollars in new investment on priority areas, including the purchase of new equipment.
At the same time, the department is still subject to reductions planned in a previous federal budget, passed by the Trudeau government.
Those reductions in operations and maintenance funding continue to roll out this year with DND expected to find $459 million in savings.
McGuinty said the controversy over the cadets and the government's decision to cut the program some budget slack is important.
"It sends the message that we are responsible with financial expenditures, that we're responsible with Canadian taxpayers' money, that we have to live within a budget," McGuinty said.
"You know, it's important for Canadians to understand there have been significant increases in funding on the defence and the Canadian Armed Forces front, but that's not a limitless amount of money."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Murray Brewster is the senior defence writer for CBC News, based in Ottawa. He has covered the Canadian military and foreign policy from Parliament Hill for over a decade. Among other assignments, he spent a total of 15 months on the ground covering the Afghan war for The Canadian Press. Prior to that, he covered defence issues and politics for CP in Nova Scotia for 11 years and was bureau chief for Standard Broadcast News in Ottawa.
